tier_reason: Benchmark code is public in attractivechaos/udb2 (common.c, khash/test.c, c++11/test.cpp, per-directory Makefiles); the README states the server CPU (Xeon E5-2683 v3) and compiler (gcc 5.4.0), and the 2018 Makefiles (khash -O2, c++11 -O3 -std=c++11, unchanged since commit 539d6d0) give the flags. The 180929-server.tgz logs contain exactly the claimed rows for khash and std::unordered_map, with identical unique-key counts and checksums across implementations.

corrections.claimed_speedup: udb2 180929 server logs (khash/run-test.log vs c++11/run-test.log): at N=50M khash 5.460 s CPU and 172.457 MB versus std::unordered_map 22.220 s and 493.762 MB, about 4.1x less CPU time and 2.9x less memory (derived from log data); at N=10M 0.652 s versus 2.972 s (4.6x, derived). The run-test-1 pair is two different variants: khash/test-1.c stores a {key,count} struct in a khash set (no separate value array), 4.724 s / 136.742 MB, while c++11/test-1.cpp uses emplace, 22.872 s / 493.363 MB at N=50M (4.8x, derived). The later 191228-server.tgz run shows the same picture: khash 4.061 s / 171.488 MB versus std::unordered_map 17.211 s / 519.270 MB at N=50M (about 4.2x CPU, 3.0x memory, derived from log data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 5.4.0 per udb2 README for the server run; khash/Makefile builds with '$(CC) -O2 -Wall' and c++11/Makefile with '$(CXX) -O3 -Wall -std=c++11' (verified in the 2018 Makefile at commit 539d6d0, unchanged in substance since), so the baseline got the higher optimization level. libstdc++ is inferred from gcc on Linux, not stated.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark lives in a separate repo (attractivechaos/udb2, same author, 35 stars, no license file) and the numbers are inside the linked tgz (udb2-lynx-log/khash/run-test.log and c++11/run-test.log); the README itself shows only plots. The 180929 run is from 2018 with gcc 5.4.0 and an old libstdc++ (unordered_map's node-based design has not changed since). udb2 vendors khash.h 0.2.8, identical to klib's current khash.h apart from comments. Only 32-bit integer keys and values (keys pre-scrambled with hash32, then an identity hash in both tables), counting workload; says nothing about string keys or lookup-only loads; a deletion variant exists for khash in 191228-server.tgz but has no std::unordered_map counterpart. The timed loop also includes key generation (about 0.12 s over the 50M sequence, small). CPU time is getrusage user+sys, single run per N. The run-test-1 pair compares a khash set-of-struct variant against an emplace-based std::unordered_map, not like for like. The README's 'results vary with machines' warning applies: the Google Cloud n1-standard-1 run uses different hardware. udb2 also lists many other maps (absl, ska, tsl, robin_hood, unordered_dense, verstable, khashl and others), most of which beat khash on the 2023 runs; khash is far from the fastest option, only clearly faster than std::unordered_map.

notes: Numbers verified line by line in 180929-server.tgz; correctness check passes (same unique-key count and checksum for khash and std::unordered_map). Corrected the second-variant description (khash run-test-1 is a set-of-struct variant) and added the 2019 server run, which agrees (about 4.2x). Baseline built at -O3 versus khash at -O2, so the comparison is not stacked in khash's favour.

tier_reason: A competitor's benchmark repo (maksimandrianov/cdcontainers.benchmarks, 1 star) with public Google Benchmark code and a stated CPU (i7-7820HQ), but no compiler version and no effective optimisation level: run.sh calls plain 'cmake ..', so the Release flags in CMakeLists.txt are not applied as published. Numbers exist only as SVG plots; the record's values match the SVG coordinates at N=122,880.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler and version not stated. CMakeLists.txt defines Release flags '-O3 -flto -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti' (C: '-O3 -flto'), but run.sh calls plain 'cmake ..' with no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so as published the benchmark binary (which instantiates the std containers) gets no -O flag, and Collections-C, built as an ExternalProject with the same empty build type, had only '-Wall -Werror' in its 2016-2019 CMakeLists.txt. Google Benchmark v1.5.0, glib 2.63.0, Collections-C pinned only to 'master' (late-2019 snapshot).
corrections.caveats: Third-party but competing: the benchmark repo belongs to the author of the rival cdcontainers library (1 star, 17 commits, last updated 2019-12-27). Numbers exist only as matplotlib SVG graphs; the figures were recovered from the SVG point coordinates (re-checked: they match). Likely unoptimised build: run.sh sets no build type, and the per-operation times at N=122,880 (about 400 ns per std::unordered_map insert, 700 ns per std::map insert, 100 ns per std::list push_back, 135 ns per std::unordered_map lookup, derived from page data) are several times what optimised libstdc++ usually achieves, which is consistent with -O0 builds where header-only C++ templates lose far more than a precompiled C library; the speedups may largely measure that, so treat them as unreliable (inference, not proven). Insert, push-front, push-back and insert-middle loops call a std::mt19937 random function per operation; search, remove and traversal use a pre-shuffled vector instead. GetRandomPos constructs uniform_int_distribution<unsigned int> from SIZE_MAX, which narrows to a = b = UINT_MAX, so the deque 'random position' is always UINT_MAX % size (deterministic, but the same for every library). The std side stores int and the C side stores int cast to void*, with std::hash<int> as the C++ hash and cdc_hash_int for the C tables. Collections-C was built from an unpinned 'master' of December 2019 using the old unprefixed API (hashtable_add, deque_add_last); the library has since been renamed to the cc_ prefix, so the benchmark code does not build against current master and the numbers predate later changes. glib's GHashTable beats CcHashTable on search and traversal, and CcTreeTable is far slower than std::unordered_map for lookups. LGPL-3.0-or-later: static linking carries relinking obligations. No std::vector comparison exists.

notes: SVG values re-derived from point coordinates and match the record (e.g., map insert CcHashTable 10.2 ms vs std::unordered_map 49.4 ms; deque random insert 337 ms vs 2560 ms). Main shortcoming: run.sh builds without a build type, and the absolute timings look like an unoptimised C++ baseline, so the ratios are untrustworthy; kept at C with the flaw documented. Metadata checked: LGPL-3.0-or-later (file headers), 3.0k stars, last commit 2026-05-12.

tier_reason: First-party plots in the README (docs/images/*.log.png) from public benchmark code (tests/perf/*/perf_*.c and .cc, driven by gen_images.sh) with compiler and flags in the plot titles (g++ 10.2.1, -O3 -march=native), but no CPU model anywhere, so not A; no numbers in text.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The README gives no ratio in text; its log-scale PNG plots show CTL as solid lines and the STL as dotted lines. Read off the plots at about 25k int elements (approximate, derived from page data): CTL roughly equal to the STL for vector, list, forward_list, set, unordered_set and priority_queue push/insert, erase and iterate, and for deque push_back and iterate; wins are str push_back about 3-4x faster than std::string push_back (about 16 us vs 60 us), priority_queue top about 7x faster (about 8 us vs 60 us for an O(1) operation) and unordered_set erase about 1.3x faster; losses are deque pop_back and pop_front about 3-4x slower (about 60 us vs 17 us), vector sort about 1.5x, deque sort about 2x, forward_list sort about 1.2x and string sort about 35x slower. The compile chart labels CTL 'tests/perf/perf_compile_c11.c' 60.12 KB and 117752k RSS against 'perf_compile_cc.cc' 43.944 KB and 153612k RSS (about 23% less compiler memory, derived from page data), with both bars at about 1.7 s.
corrections.caveats: This is a weak claim: the project's stated goal is STL-compatible C containers with security and verification features, and the plots show parity rather than wins, with sorts and deque pops clearly slower. The README says only 'C is roughly comparable to C++'; the unordered_set doc says 'Overall the STL unordered_set performance is bad, and our is also not much better.' The compile chart shows equal compile time (about 1.7 s each) and a larger stripped CTL binary (60.12 KB vs 43.944 KB), with only compiler memory lower. No ratio appears in text; all figures were read off embedded PNG plots, so they are approximate. The plots were last regenerated in February-March 2021 (last docs/images commit 2021-03-26, GCC 10.2.1), so they predate about five years of changes (new hashmap policies, swisstable work in 2026); the str and set graphs are not in gen_images.sh's default list. Hardware is not stated; each point is a single wall-clock run per size; results are first-party. Only int (and char for str) elements are measured. As the README notes, the C++ functions are partly dynamically loaded from libstdc++.so.6 while the C versions are compiled into the binary. GitHub shows the repo as forked from glouw/ctl; the README lists a renamed API and 254 methods as improvements over the original.

notes: Plots read directly: parity overall, a few CTL wins (str push_back, pqu top, uset erase) and several losses (deque pop_back/pop_front about 3-4x slower, all sorts slower). Record's claimed_speedup missed the deque pop losses and the pqu top win; corrected. Tier C stays (no CPU model); plots are from 2021. Fork of glouw/ctl confirmed on the GitHub page; MIT, 288 stars, last commit 2026-09-25.
